When I received that complaint a week ago Thursday I immediately investigated the matter, as I have told the hon. member. On that Saturday I was in New Brunswick myself. I was not at Campbellton or Edmundston, but I did take steps to satisfy myself that there was no undue delay.
I returned to my office and on Monday morning I received this wire, dated Campbellton, February 18. It is addressed to me:
Unless immediate action is taken to remove the bottleneck and mixup in Campbellton unemployment office I seriously fear that a riot will occur very soon. Seasonal workers are up in arms and many are experiencing delays of up to six weeks while their families live in utter poverty. Immediate action is required by you.
J. C. Van Horne
I am sure this is a matter which, since it affects two municipalities in New Brunswick and workers who are fellow New Bruns-wickers, is one that particularly affects the hon. member and myself. I should like to have the opportunity of explaining to him through you, and to the house, that no steps were left untaken to see that there was no hardship being experienced by the workers in those two communities.
The commission told me that since the usual New Year's rush several weeks ago, both offices had been able to bring their work well up to date. About the day the hon. member made his complaint there was only a total of nine claims uncompleted which were over three weeks old, and these were being dealt with; some of them were under adjudication by a board of referees.

Inquiries of the Ministry I was informed also that there was no evidence of confusion at either office.
These things I was prepared to convey to the house last Monday when I received the wire which I have read to the house. When I received that wire I again checked through the unemployment insurance commission. After another inquiry they told me there were no serious delays in these offices. I told them I had received contrary information from a source which I was bound to consider completely responsible.

We of the official opposition have made our position clear. We are opposed to this legislation. The right hon. In support of his statement the minister said that he had visited western Canada and that almost on every hand the attitude of the farmers was that this was a good legislation.
I did not find such an attitude among the farmers in my constituency or in those portions of Saskatchewan which I visited. In every case, and there was no exception, I found the sternest opposition being expressed to this legislation in that in effect it means that the farmer is substituting one debt for other debts, and is paying interest on his earnings in the preceding year, something that cannot be justified in any way.
The government has tried piecemeal means to meet the demands of the western farmers. First it brought into effect legislation by an order in council allowing farmers to exchange good wheat for poor wheat being stored in the elevators. That legislation was proclaimed as the solution of the problem of storage facilities being used to store wheat that was more or less unsaleable. Mr. Speaker, when this bill was first introduced into the house, we in this group objected at every opportunity. In doing so we stated we did not believe that the principle involved in the bill was going to fulfil the requirements of the situation. We do not believe that the farmers can borrow themselves into prosperity. We do not believe that the farmers can borrow themselves out of debt.
Certainly the clauses and the conditions that were discussed in connection with this bill the other day would lead us to believe that our decision to oppose this legislation was completely justified. By amending certain clauses the government gave evidence that it saw in many instances that the clauses were unrealistic. Of course we maintain and always have maintained that both the bill and the clauses were unrealistic, because of the government's misunderstanding of the true situation farmers in western Canada are facing.
It seems that in drafting the clauses and the conditions the government did everything possible to discourage farmers from taking advantage, if there was any advantage, of this legislation, rather than encouraging them to do so. Certainly the risk that was involved in this legislation with regard to interest did not seem to be warranted. Certainly, on the admission of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, from the 1951 experience it would seem that even at that time there was very little risk involved.
When we consider the difference between the circumstances that exist today and those that existed in 1951, surely the risk today has been almost completely eliminated. In 1951, as we know, the grain was out in the field, and there was a considerable risk involved in loaning money under those conditions. Now the conditions are different. As far as the quality and condition of the grain are concerned, the farmers have harvested possibly the best crop they have had for several years. So we believe that the risk involved certainly does not warrant the 5 per cent interest charge being levied in this case. By increasing the guarantees to the banks, any risk the banks might take are completely ruled out. By the same token the government leaves no question regarding risk, in so far as any of the other aspects are concerned. As I mentioned a moment ago, the grain is in good condition, and I see no reason why there should be an interest rate of 5 per cent.
In regard to the penalties under clause 9, the government again realized how unrealistic this was, and was prepared to make certain amendments to that clause. When we read clause 9 as it was presented to this 67509-103J
Grain
house, we cannot help thinking the government feels that the farmer must be quite a questionable character as far as living up to obligations of repayment is concerned, because clause 9 left no risk whatsoever with regard to repayment by the farmer.
Every one of the clauses seemed to be purposely provided to limit the uses of this bill, and went a long way to discourage farmers from taking advantage of it. Listening to the Minister of Agriculture, who just returned from a trip to the west, one gets the impression that he is convinced in his own mind that farmers are quite happy and quite satisfied with this legislation. He mentioned in particular the information he had that the farmers in my riding were quite satisfied with it, and he gave as evidence of that the fact that he talked to a certain individual in Winnipeg.
My guess is that he was much more concerned about the coming provincial election in Saskatchewan, and I presume he went out there to oil the old Gardiner machine. Certainly he still has lots of oil, but the parts Of the machine are not as new as they used to be. The minister prophesied that those who had spoken against the legislation in the house will go back to Saskatchewan and sing a different tune, but he should disabuse his mind completely of that idea because we intend to go back and talk exactly the same in the west as we have talked in the east. There will be no difference, and I am sure nobody in the house knows better than the minister that that is exactly what we are going to do.
As I mentioned in the first instance, we have consistently opposed the legislation. We do not believe it is just in principle, and we can see now that so far as carrying out the provisions of the legislation is concerned, the government has done everything possible to make sure that it is not going to give the assistance that is necessary. On third reading of the bill we in this group will continue to oppose the legislation, and once again I take the opportunity to say on behalf of the group I represent that our opposition is as adamant as ever.

But I want to make it quite clear that our position in regard to cash advances without interest has been consistent right through, and since long before this arose. In fact it is more than three years since we urged the introduction of legislation which would provide such advances with the authority of parliament, not under some letter written by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) to authorize the banks to do something which had not yet been authorized by parliament.
I do want to mention one particular matter which I think should be of concern to everyone in this house. One of the points we brought forward early in this discussion and in regard to which there has been no statement whatever by the government is the need of some clear statement to the prairie farmers as to what their position is going to be only six months from now, when the 1956 crop is going to be harvested.
That suggestion very much amuses the Minister of Finance. Of course his chuckles are not recorded on Hansard, but it will be recognized by hon. members that the Minister of Finance regards the plight of the prairie farmer as something funny when this suggestion is made.
I want to point out that as yet no explanation has been given as to what the government proposes to do. The Minister of Finance need not pretend that all government action is in suspense until his august voice has been raised on the budget. After all, this government did not hesitate to commit parliament while parliament was not sitting. This government did not hesitate to have the Minister of Finance commit this parliament by a letter. Then we were told by the Minister of Trade and Commerce that since that had been done, the government was going to go ahead with it no matter what arguments were made.

1 hope no suggestion will be put forward that section 13, subsection 1 of this act is an answer to that question. That subsection reads:
The governor in council may, by order, extend the application of this act to authorize and govern guaranteed loans that may be made by banks on or after the 1st day of October, 1956 and before the 1st day of June, 1957.
We have had no indication from the government as to whether it would be their intention under this act to extend those provisions if the same conditions prevail this coming autumn as prevail at this time. Our position is that inadequate though that may be, we should know whether the government feels that this will meet the situation if on top of the large crops we have had we have another bumper crop this year, as we may well have with the weather conditions we have been experiencing in western Canada during the past few months.
The prairie farmer is going to be in a most uncertain and precarious position in planning for his coming crop year unless he has some indication from this government at this time of what it proposes to do. There is no more appropriate time for that statement to be made than on the third reading of this bill, before it becomes law and is made a part of the statutes of Canada. Therefore at this stage I once again point out that we have had no indication of the intentions of the government.
I point out that it is of the utmost importance to the prairie farmers that an indication be given as to what are the intentions of the government. It is no answer to say that under subsection 1 of section 13 the government would have the power. Let the government tell us whether they will exercise that power if conditions are similar to what they are now, or if they have been aggravated by another very large crop.
The opportunity presents itself for the government to make this statement now. May I repeat that whether the government makes that statement or not, the government is still failing the prairie farmers. One of the best possible pieces of evidence that it is failing the prairie farmers is the fact that it is necessary for it to bring in other legislation, with which we shall deal after this has been disposed of. The fact is that the other legislation, which will receive the support of the house, has become necessary simply because of the failure of this government to move the wheat crop, a failure with which they must deal in that way.
So far as this legislation is concerned, before it passes third reading and goes forward to become law, let us hear from the
Grain
government as to what their intentions are under that clause which they have drafted, clause 13 (1), and whether it is their intention to extend the application of this bill if conditions remain similar to what they now are.

Criminal Code
arising out of the pollution of interprovincial streams in Canada. In the case of navigable streams offences are created in so far as the Fisheries Act is concerned when anything in the nature of an effluent and the like is dumped into a stream and causes harm to fish; but in so far as interprovincial rivers are concerned, as the law stands today there is practical immunity for those who dump effluents into the river because of the wording of the section in question which permits wanton and wilful pollution of streams when there is no effect upon the health and comfort of the individual.
There are many examples of this, one outstanding example being the majestic Ottawa river which adjoins these parliament buildings. I believe that in the realm of God's richest bounty clean river water should have a high place and ought not to be allowed to be sacrificed to private greed or to wanton and wilful pollution. There is nothing today in the law to protect the public against wanton and wilful pollution by a small minority who for their own purposes contemptuously disregard the public interest in so far as interprovincial rivers are concerned.
This problem has been before the house on two previous occasions. At the time the amendments to the Criminal Code were before the house I placed before hon. members details of a situation which had arisen on the North Saskatchewan river whereby the residents of North Battleford and Prince Albert in Saskatchewan and The Pas in Manitoba were for a long period of time unable to utilize the waters of that great river because of acts of pollution taking place in the province of Alberta. Those acts of pollution took place east of Edmonton and because there was little or no interference with personal enjoyment of those waters in the province of Alberta we in Prince Albert found ourselves in the position where there was little or nothing we could do to protect our people-the same applied to North Battleford and The Pas-from the action of those who were pouring effluents into the stream in Alberta.

It is not what you might call a pastel picture.
There is no way of meeting this problem from the provincial point of view. I think it was the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) who suggested that there would be a right to proceed by way of injunction in the province of origin because of effects created in an adjoining province on an interprovincial river. An eminent counsel, a former president of the Canadian Bar Association, Mr. McCuaig, Q. C., of Edmonton, has said that he knows of no such right under the law as it is now constituted.
The situation in the United States became so serious that in 1948 a federal board was set up. In that country the criminal law rests with the state. The federal control board in combination with those who implement the criminal law in the several states has been able to meet this problem in part.
It is because this problem must be faced that I bring this amendment before the house. If it is not faced, in a very few years all over Canada interprovincial streams will be subject to the same pollution as the Ottawa river is today and as the North Saskatchewan river is rapidly becoming. When this matter was before the house beginning on March 18, 1955, the Minister of Justice claimed that it was a matter for the provinces. I face that challenge immediately and point out this fact: Not only is there no right for anyone in Manitoba to take proceedings even though he is adversely affected by the waters of the Saskatchewan flowing into his province because of what takes place in Saskatchewan; there is no means by which provinces can achieve that degree of united purpose which would meet this problem. In the month of July, the city of Ottawa asked the federal government to investigate the pollution situation on the Ottawa river. On July 14, 1955,
[Mr. Diefenbaker.)
I brought this matter up in a question recorded on page 6109 of Hansard as follows:
I should like to direct a question to the Prime Minister. Has the government received an application from the corporation of the city of Ottawa to investigate the pollution situation in the Ottawa river? Is it the intention of the government to set up a commission to investigate the question of pollution of navigable waters? If so, would the Prime Minister give consideration as well to having any commission investigating the serious pollution situation in the Ottawa river also include interprovincial rivers in other parts of Canada?
The Prime Minister used these words:
I have received no application yet from the city of Ottawa although I have read newspaper reports, which are frequently ahead of the actual accomplishments that they seem to be reporting. The matter of water pollution is a matter of concern to all forward-looking Canadians. We are going to have a larger population in this country than we have at the present time. It is a serious matter because, of course, pure water is essential to the comfort of the population. Nothing specific has been done about it yet but we are all thinking of what will be the best way to assure even to future generations that the bountiful supply of water with which nature has endowed this country is going to be available in potable form for their use.
I commend those words. They represent a statesmanlike view of the situation and of the need for action. That was on July 14, 1955. I then asked the Prime Minister a further question:
Would the Prime Minister say whether or not some amendment to the Criminal Code in order to punish wrong-doing of the kind might be within the consideration of the government?
The Prime Minister said:
All means should be explored and considered seriously to achieve the desired objective. I would not like at this time to say that the federal government is going to take the initiative. It is normally, or has been in the past normally, a matter of local and private interest for each locality. We do not want to be looked upon as going beyond what is reasonably within our jurisdiction. I regard it as something that is of concern not only locally but nationally for the future of the country. I am sure it is something which will be discussed, or at least will be talked about, at the next federal-provincial meeting. I think it will be possible to create an atmosphere where no one will regard the other one's activities as overstepping what he should be concerned about.
In that statement the Prime Minister said that it has normally been a matter of local interest. I immediately challenged that suggestion with reference to an interprovincial river. It is of more than local interest. When a river crosses the boundary lines of one or two provinces it immediately becomes the concern of the federal government. The federal government concerns itself over the comfort and health of fish in that type of river. Is it too much to ask that the same regard be given to the demands of human beings? Certainly the situation is very serious.

In Prince Albert today we are back in a position in regard to which, if I were to read some of the descriptive words about the nature of the pollution of the water in that city of 20,000 population, I would certainly be regarded as using unparliamentary words. I am taking the north Saskatchewan as an example because I live there. The situation is so serious that on two occasions for over two months one could not take water out of the tap. The stench was such that it was impossible to utilize that water. The situation is bad again this year but not as serious as it was two years ago. That is because one of the corporations has made a great effort and gone to great expense in order to remove its contribution to the pollution of that stream. The Prince Albert Daily Herald described it in these words on January 18 of this year in an editorial:
That we should be subjected to this annual scourge of polluted water is a crime, we are all in agreement. It is on the question of what can be done about it that opinion loses unanimity.
I am not going to read what has been done. There has been a great deal of co-operation on the part of the government of Alberta with the government of Saskatchewan and with the authorities in Saskatchewan, but the problem still remains. I repeat that it cannot be met through the courts under the law as it now stands. I mentioned Mr. McCuaig's opinion. I quote from the-

I met with Mr. McCualg, who was our legal counsel in Edmonton, during the 1953 pollution outbreak. He informed me of the legal difficulty of a city in one province obtaining an injunction against a city in another province, and stated that as yet he has found no legal method by which this can be accomplished.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING POLLUTION OF INTERPROVINCIAL RIVERS
speechtext: May I ask my hon. friend if we are clear that Mr. McCuaig's opinion did not deal with an invocation of the Criminal Code section dealing with common nuisance? I had rather understood my hon. friend on a previous occasion in this house to indicate that Mr. McCuaig had expressed an opinion that the nuisance section in its present form could not be invoked. Apparently that is not the case.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING POLLUTION OF INTERPROVINCIAL RIVERS
speechtext:
My hon. friend will again bring up that argument. I am saying that there is no civil recourse, and it should not
Criminal Code
be necessary on an interprovincial scheme to have active and wanton pollution whereby people are denied the God-given water that in the years to come will become less and less available to the people of this country because of the improper acts of those who disregard the rights of others. There has been only one case on the subject since we dealt with this on the last occasion; that is an outstanding judgment by Mr. Justice Caron in the district of Montreal, in the case of Jacques Drouin and the city of Dorval. In that judgment, for the first time the judge goes as far as to determine that riparian owners on navigable waters have a right of action; but nowhere is there any authority for the right of an individual on an interprovincial river that is not a navigable stream within the meaning of the federal legislation applicable to navigable streams in this country.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING POLLUTION OF INTERPROVINCIAL RIVERS
speechtext: My hon. friend is now speaking about civil action.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING POLLUTION OF INTERPROVINCIAL RIVERS
speechtext:
That is what I am saying. I am saying there is no civil right and that therefore there must be something in the nature of criminal proceedings. That is what I am leading up to. There is not such a right today under the criminal law. The opinion of counsel has been given that the section in question, dealing with nuisance, does not allow for any proceedings being taken under the Criminal Code as now constituted.
Having first pointed out that the person has no civil rights on an interprovincial river whose water supply has been polluted, I am now endeavouring, following that, to show that the only means is to put teeth in the criminal law so that wrongdoers who would take advantage of the situation and thereby destroy this bounty of nature shall be severely punished. I have a description here of the terrible conditions prevalent on the Ottawa river. It is to be found in an article by Reg. R. Fife in the January, 1955 issue of Rod and Gun. He points out that today, as far as the Ottawa river is concerned, less than 150 miles of water takes the domestic and industrial sewage, including all effluents, of 800,000 people and several large polluting industries, or the sewage of 5,000 people per mile of river. The article goes on to say:
Now polluting industries are quick to point out that their effluent or waste waters have no harmful bacteria and so are not dangerous to public health. However, the power of the water to assimilate and destroy the bacteria ... is decreased because the water uses its oxygen to oxidize the industrial wastes.
I can see no reason why the attitude of the minister has been in opposition to such an amendment being made. Last year he raised

Criminal Code
objection to the fact that my amendment did not include municipal pollution. That was done for a purpose. Municipal pollution is a matter for each of the provincial health departments. The responsibility to assure that municipalities shall live up to the law becomes a matter of individual concern to the several departments of health in the several provinces. But so far as an interprovincial stream is concerned there is no responsibility on anyone, and why the minister should take the stand that a matter of serious moment such as pollution should not be covered by an amendment to the Criminal Code is rather difficult to understand. Indeed, in the March, 1956, issue of Rod and Gun there is an editorial that sums up the situation and I adopt what it says therein. It reads:
Before the House of Commons as we go to press is a bill which would make it a criminal offence to pollute interprovincial waterways beyond the point of human safety and comfort.
Then it goes on to say what the suggested fine is.
Rod and Gun readers will remember that pollution from the area of the city of Edmonton swept down the 400 miles of the North Saskatchewan river to Prince Albert in neighbouring Saskatchewan. It so affected the taste and purity of the water there that residents of P.A. were quite rightly up in arms over the whole thing. The water was unfit for human consumption-especially if you were the human that had to drink it. It is also almost certain that it had killed every game fish in the river over that 400 miles . . . There was enough evidence of dead fish around the P.A. water intake to further disturb the residents of that fine city.
In all the uproar that followed . . . the most significant thing to come out was that there is no legal machinery to properly handle pollution of interprovincial waterways. In fairness to the firm in Edmonton that some investigators feel was responsible for the first outburst it must be stated that they have, without any pressure from anyone, spent over $150,000 to try to reduce the noxious properties of the waste water they discharge into the river. However, just because one firm has done this is no guarantee that others will follow suit. And it may be stated with certainty that more than one Edmonton industry is discharging polluting substances into that river, just as there is more than one industry responsible for the deplorable situation on the once magnificent Ottawa river . . .
This problem is quite different legally from that posed by pollution entirely within provincial boundaries which then becomes a provincial matter unless the offence involves those waters affected by the Fisheries Act, regulations under the Migratory Birds Convention Act, national harbours board regulations concerning the protection of navigable waters or regulations under the Canada Shipping Act.
Certainly there is a lot to be done within provincial boundaries, and in every province in Canada, where a shirking of responsibilities on the part of elected officials combined with a base display of public apathy has given us a situation that is close to desperate in several areas.
The Canadian parliament has before it a bill which can correct a long standing and evil situation. . . . For these public waters do not belong
[Mr. Diefenbaker.j
to us. They are there for us to use and to enjoy, for us to build a great nation upon. But they are not ours to defile and to destroy. They are a part of the priceless heritage it is our duty and our privilege to pass on to other generations of Canadians.
That in general is the representation I wish to make in support of the amendment I suggest. It will put teeth in the law. As the law stands today there is no right under section 165, the present nuisance section, or any other section of the Criminal Code, to prosecute wrongdoers on interprovincial rivers. All that section will do is to cover the individual who dumps a bit of stuff into a river within the province in which the prosecution takes place. But nowhere and under no authority can anything be done by people living in provinces adjoining the province in which the pollution has taken place. The penalty-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING POLLUTION OF INTERPROVINCIAL RIVERS
speechtext: I wonder whether my hon. friend would permit a question at this point? Under the amendment to the Code which he proposes, if someone in Edmonton were guilty of an offence under it, which offence caused difficulty in Prince Albert, would he not agree that the prosecution of that offence would have to be conducted by the Alberta law enforcement authorities?

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING POLLUTION OF INTERPROVINCIAL RIVERS
speechtext: I do not have before me the section of the Criminal Code that covers exactly that type of thing where an offence happens affecting two jurisdictions. One of the earlier general sections of the Criminal Code provides for eventualities similar to that; but whether or not my hon. friend is correct, suppose the pollution took place in the province of Alberta: all that would need to be done would be for a charge to be laid in the province of Alberta and the witnesses transported to the place of trial within Alberta.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING POLLUTION OF INTERPROVINCIAL RIVERS
speechtext: May I ask my hon. friend another question? If that be so, then would not the same condition of affairs and the same reasoning apply to a charge for committing a common nuisance which had been committed in Alberta, which caused a bad effect in Prince Albert and which could be prosecuted in Alberta by taking Saskatchewan witnesses to Alberta for that purpose?

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING POLLUTION OF INTERPROVINCIAL RIVERS
speechtext:
With that general proposition I am not in agreement. In making pollution on interprovincial rivers a criminal offence I think the prosecution could be taken in either place, where the pollution actually took place or in the province in which the effects of that pollution were felt. The ordinary nuisance section as it now stands reads:
Every one who commits a common nuisance and thereby

(a)	endangers the lives, safety or health of the public, or
(b)	causes physical injury to any person . . .
II the section as it now stands covered cases such as this, then a person in Prince Albert or any other place in Saskatchewan affected by the pollution would be able to take a prosecution against the Alberta company. But as the law now stands, there is no provision whatsoever. That is not my opinion, although I entirely concur in it; that is the opinion of counsel. Under the law as it now stands, there is nothing that can be done by a resident in one province to meet the nuisance of pollution in an adjoining province.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING POLLUTION OF INTERPROVINCIAL RIVERS
speechtext: Would my hon. friend permit a question at that point?

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING POLLUTION OF INTERPROVINCIAL RIVERS
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING POLLUTION OF INTERPROVINCIAL RIVERS

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING POLLUTION OF INTERPROVINCIAL RIVERS
speechtext: I have already said it is the general principle covered by the general law and set out in detail in the earlier portions of the Criminal Code.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker-

speechtext:
Just wait a minute. I have already said that under the section as it now stands proceedings could be taken in Prince Albert if the present nuisance section covered the situation. I say that it does not cover that situation because pollution of an interprovincial stream does not come within the law as it is now constituted. It is because of that fact that I want this amendment added so as to cover interprovincial streams. Then immediately there will be available the right of action and there will also be teeth in the law.
As the matter stands today the maximum penalty-even if the present section applied -on indictment is two years or the matter could be proceeded with by way of summary conviction in which case the maximum penalty would be $500. But $500 penalties, even if they were applicable, would be simply nothing to corporations which wantonly and wilfully pollute these waters. I go back to this principle, and I am trying to make it clear to my hon. friend. As the law is now, or as the section reads now, there is no right of action for the pollution of interprovincial rivers. The amendment will make it an offence.
However, if my hon. friend wants to take the stand that the present section meets the
Criminal Code
situation, then I ask him why he stands so firmly against an added section which will reinforce what he says is already there. Last year he took a different stand. Last year he took the stand that this was not a matter for the criminal law at all, in spite of the fact that that is the manner in which the United States has met the situation. It has met it, first, by a federal board and second, by each of the states having the authority over the criminal law joining in punishing those guilty of pollution of interstate streams.
My hon. friend cannot have it both ways. If he says the law today covers the situation, my answer to him is that no counsel who has been retained anywhere has come to that conclusion. If on the other hand-

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING POLLUTION OF INTERPROVINCIAL RIVERS

speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING POLLUTION OF INTERPROVINCIAL RIVERS
speechtext: Were not the opinions which were given by counsel based upon a stated set of facts relating to the question that was presented to them and were the opinions not dealing with those facts and not with a general statement of the law?

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING POLLUTION OF INTERPROVINCIAL RIVERS
speechtext:
As a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker, as an eminent counsel yourself you know that the only way in which counsel can come to an opinion is on the basis of the facts. There is nothing intricate about the facts in this case as far as Saskatchewan is concerned. The people cannot drink the water. Pollution takes place a few miles east of Edmonton. Those are simple facts. They are known facts. They are obvious facts. On the basis of those simple facts, unclouded in any way by any other considerations or any doubt as to the existence of any of those facts, counsel has advised that there is no right of action because this is an interprovincial stream and the section as it now stands does not meet the situation of pollution under those circumstances.
If my hon. friend were to say that possibly counsel did not get all the facts or that they might have been misstated, I would reply that there can be no mistake here. The simplicity of the facts is such that a child could understand them. The water is polluted. The people cannot drink it. They live on a river. They trace the pollution back to five miles or ten miles east of Edmonton. They establish that the pollution in fact took place there and on an earlier occasion. Those facts are simplicity itself. Upon those facts counsel gave his opinion.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING POLLUTION OF INTERPROVINCIAL RIVERS
speechtext: Of course, Mr. Speaker, this is just a smokescreen, if I may say so with all due respect. On proceedings being taken, if the evidence was not available, then whether the law was changed or not, the result would not be a conviction. But accepting the facts that wrongdoing by pollution took place east of Edmonton and that the pollution which took place caused the noxious water in Prince Albert, counsel's opinion, on the basis of those facts, was that there is no right of action. He went even further and gave the opinion that there would be no civil right of action in our province for the wrong done in Alberta nor in the Alberta courts for the wrong done in Saskatchewan by an Alberta company.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING POLLUTION OF INTERPROVINCIAL RIVERS
speechtext: What does my hon. friend think of that opinion?

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING POLLUTION OF INTERPROVINCIAL RIVERS
speechtext: I accept counsel's opinion. I do not place myself above a former president of the Canadian Bar Association.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING POLLUTION OF INTERPROVINCIAL RIVERS
speechtext: Do you agree with it?

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING POLLUTION OF INTERPROVINCIAL RIVERS
speechtext:
As a matter of fact, I agree that there is no right of criminal action and I take counsel's advice that there is no right of civil action. As a matter of fact, if you read the Caron judgment, you will find that while it says there is a right of action on navigable streams, it raises grave doubts as to whether on other streams there is any right of action. This is a most interesting judgment. I am not going into the facts. I have quoted the case so that anyone may read it. How doubtful the law is is indicated by the fact that this is the first case in which a riparian owner on a navigable stream has

been upheld in an action arising out of pollution. That is the first case in which such a thing has happened. The judge did not arrive at that judgment without considerable doubt with regard to several of the conclusions to which he came. If there is any doubt as to the right of civil action, I ask why it is that the government is standing so adamant against giving people a little bit of protection under the Criminal Code.
They protect you under the Criminal Code for petty pollutions, for common nuisances. I should like to know. Is it because there are some strong interests that are opposed? Is it because some strong interests realize that if teeth are put into the law those interests are going to be placed in a position where no longer may they wantonly disregard the rights of ordinary citizens? Is that why? When the situation is as serious as the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) admitted last July, as serious as it now is-and in years to come it will become more and more serious-I put it to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson): why, in the face of the actions of individuals or corporations which put the public welfare at naught, does the government have such a resolute, such a relentless stand?
If my hon. friend says the amendment may not cover all the situations now, further amendments could take place. But give to the ordinary citizen in Canada this amendment and it will not be long before great corporations will realize that the public interest will hold them responsible under the code. I have exhausted my time, sir, but I do hope that the government has changed its attitude a little since last year, although I must say, having regard to the interruptions of the minister, it seems apparent to me that the crime of wilful pollution is still to be outside the ambit of the Criminal Code. I do hope he will give more consideration to it than he did last year, and thereby enable the preservation of one of the greatest resources that we have. Think of the magnificent Ottawa river, famed in legend and in history, and then think of it today, almost an open sewer because it is interprovincial. Surely that situation is but another example that calls for resolute action. The only way to do it is to put the fear of possible punishment in the hearts of those who would wantonly destroy God's greatest gift to mankind.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING POLLUTION OF INTERPROVINCIAL RIVERS
speechtext:
I had not intended to take part in this debate, but while listening to the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) a thought came to my mind which I felt I should put on Hansard and bring to the attention of the hon. member. I do not believe the solution

he proposes would be a practical one. It is not a solution for the difficulties that exist. It is not a proper method of preventing the pollution that is now taking place. I appreciate, as he does, the importance of the problem. He has indicated it to us very clearly.
But while listening to him I could not help thinking of the great pulp and paper industry in Canada, and especially in my province. When I think of the importance of that industry which produces 6 million tons of newsprint, of which 3 million are produced in my province, I cannot help but ask myself what would be the result of the legislation advocated by the hon. member. A good many of the mills engaged in the paper industry are situated on interprovincial streams. The object of my hon. friend would evidently be to prevent them from polluting the waters of these interprovincial streams. Unfortunately these mills cannot operate without dumping into the waters that run near the mill all sorts of refuse which, according to the definition of the amendment proposed to the Criminal Code, would be illegal. The amendment reads:
Every owner, lessee, or person operating any industrial plant, oil refinery, chemical works, sawmill . . . who discharges or throws or allows to be discharged or thrown any noxious waste product, raw sewage, oil, sawdust, chemical or other matter or thing into a river . . .
No paper mill can operate without getting rid of the chemicals that have to be used in the manufacture of paper. Those chemicals have to run away in the water near the mill.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING POLLUTION OF INTERPROVINCIAL RIVERS
speechtext: Would the hon. member permit a question?

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING POLLUTION OF INTERPROVINCIAL RIVERS
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING POLLUTION OF INTERPROVINCIAL RIVERS
speechtext: He raises a very challenging point, but is it not a fact a similar situation has been met in the United States by demanding that those companies use proper destructive measures to neutralize the noxious properties of the things that they dump into the streams.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING POLLUTION OF INTERPROVINCIAL RIVERS
speechtext:
I do not think it has been found possible, from a practical point of view, to do those things. In any case, there are also the waste wood products apart from the chemicals that flow into these waters.
My point is that the remedy suggested by my hon. friend would not be a practical one because it only consists of fines. Supposing you did condemn these paper companies to pay a fine. You could condemn them again and they would pay another fine. If you wanted them to observe the law to the letter and be absolutely immune from penalties, you would force them to close down. No
Criminal Code
one wants to see this great paper industry which produces 6 million tons of newsprint, a large percentage of which is exported, closed down. Everyone will agree to that. Therefore, I say it is not a practical solution. Some practical solution might be found if a committee were established to find a solution. But I say that simply passing a law to say that dumping refuse or matter into a river that pollutes it is illegal is not a solution to the problem. For that reason, I shall vote against the amendment if there is a vote called.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING POLLUTION OF INTERPROVINCIAL RIVERS
speechtext:
I am
interested in this particular problem, Mr. Speaker, for the same reason that the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) is. I would correct him in one respect. I understood him to say that the water of the city of North Battleford had been polluted, but that is not exactly true. It is the town of Battleford that suffered from water pollution and not the city of North Battleford.
There was a lot of discussion and many questions were asked of the cabinet ministers during 1954 when the pollution of the North Saskatchewan river took place. It seemed to be almost impossible to establish what should be done to stop the pollution. We have not that immediate problem at the moment. The province of Alberta and the one chemical plant that was responsible for the pollution at that time have been doing good work. The question of pollution is not a problem today. There is always a chance of a recurrence. As I said last year, if we get another government in the province of Alberta or if that government gets lazy and careless and allows industry or whoever it is who dumps their refuse into rivers to get out of hand we will still have that same problem recurring.
The minister made a suggestion in 1954 which I thought was a good one. The people in my home constituency also thought it was a good one. We tried at that time to set up an interprovincial body to look after the water of the three western provinces. Two of the provinces were willing to work with that combination of the three provinces but one province refused to do so.
The only comeback that anyone has, as far as I can see, is to take action through the Criminal Code. This is probably a debate for lawyers rather than for laymen, but looking at it from a common-sense point of view, section 165 of the act is pretty vague. I know the minister takes a pretty definite stand as to its being strong enough but I would remind the minister that when the pollution took place in the city of Prince Albert in 1954 it took a long time to find out what the cause was and where the source was. Both the hon.

Criminal Code
member for Prince Albert and I asked questions of the Minister of Fisheries, the Minister of National Health and Welfare and others. We asked all the ministers we could think of who might be connected with the problem as well as the Prime Minister. I can recall the Minister of National Health and Welfare saying on many occasions how complicated the whole matter was and how difficult it was to put the blame on any particular industry that was located 400 miles away.
The amendment to the Criminal Code that has been proposed reads as follows:
Every owner, lessee, or person operating any industrial plant, oil refinery, chemical works, sawmill or other plant or works, or any other person, who discharges or throws or allows to be discharged or thrown any noxious waste product, raw sewage, oil, sawdust, chemical or other matter or thing into a river, stream or other water ahy part of which is interprovincial or which flows into any interprovincial water, which has the effect of endangering the lives, safety, health or comfort of the public is guilty-
It seems to me that it would be far easier for any lawyer or any court to find the source of the pollution and to get to the source of the pollution if this amendment were adopted. They will see that one industry is dumping refuse or that a certain city is doing so. They can see with their own eyes and the evidence is right there.

At six o'clock the house took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The house resumed at eight o'clock.

The house resumed, from Thursday, February 9, consideration of the motion of the Prime Minister:
That a select committee to be designated be appointed to consider such of the estimates as may be referred to it and to report from time to time its findings and recommendations to the house.

Mr. Speaker, when this motion standing in the name of the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) for the appointment of a select committee to consider certain estimates was before the house some days ago I spoke briefly and in the course of my remarks dealt with the origin and purpose of the committee as they were revealed to us, at least in another
Committee on Estimates parliament, the parliament of the United Kingdom, and also with some of the thoughts expressed in this parliament when we first decided to set up such a committee.
I suggested that the proper purpose was not so much to relieve parliament as a whole of work as to enable parliament better to accomplish its job of reviewing government expenditures. In that connection I think I can say fairly that all are agreed that for the task of making a detailed review of the estimates the committee of supply is a somewhat cumbersome method of proceeding. Therefore it has been decided, if I interpret the feeling of the house correctly, that this committee should be set up which will make a detailed examination of such departments as may be referred to it and that in the course of those examinations it should do the job which the committee of the whole house sitting as the committee of supply cannot do.
What I want to suggest this evening in the few minutes remaining to me is that the special committee on estimates, as set up last year and as envisaged in the motion presented to us by the right hon. Prime Minister, cannot do the job which parliament desires should be done. It cannot do the job because it is much too limited and circumscribed by its terms of reference. The motion reads:
That a select committee to be designated be appointed to consider such of the estimates as may be referred to it and to report from time to time its findings and recommendations to the house.
There are certain very obvious limitations upon the power of that committee if the committee is appointed only on the basis of that motion. The first and most obvious limitation is that the committee will have no power to call for persons, papers and records; it will have no power to call witnesses. The second obvious limitation is that the committee will have before it for consideration only such estimates as the government by the control of its majority in the house may refer to it. I think in those two respects the committee will be seriously hampered in its job of making a detailed, impartial and independent examination of the estimates.
We saw last year in the work of the committee which was set up then for the first time, and which it is true operated to some extent on an experimental basis, just what those particular limitations meant. Let us take the first limitation I mentioned, namely that the committee has no power to call witnesses. What does that mean? It means that all that is to be presented to the committee is the evidence which the government is prepared to have presented to it. That was our experience last year.
