Committee on Estimates
We moved in committee that we be given the power to send for persons, papers and records, and that motion was denied. That motion and different variations of that motion were moved on a number of occasions and each time it was denied because the government spokesman on the committee said it was not the government's intention that we should have the right to hear anyone but the people the government wanted to present to us.
So what happened? I was a member of the committee while it was reviewing the estimates of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration. The Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Pickersgill) had himself made a member of the committee. Every time we asked for power to call witnesses the minister said it was not desirable or necessary that we should call for witnesses, that he and his departmental officials were prepared to answer all questions we might lay before the committee. Well, sir, I know and you know as a practical politician that the only witnesses whom the department was prepared to submit to the committee were those who-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I object at the present moment to being referred to as a practical politician.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Your Honour is not an impractical one.

Your Honour is neither impractical nor unversed in the art of practising politics. Your Honour does not practise them in this house but you know what is meant by the term practical politician. What happened was what could be expected to happen. We got only those witnesses that the government was prepared to allow to come before us, and those witnesses were to say only those things which the government was prepared to have them say. So far as an independent expression of opinion in the operation of government departments was concerned, its ability to obtain an expression of opinion which did not reflect the government's point of view with respect to the operation of the department, the committee was completely ineffectual.
I think we should contrast the method of operation of the estimates committee in the United Kingdom. There the committee is master of its own procedure. It is true that on the committee there is a majority from the government party which is natural in the composition of a committee made up of members of the house, but they have established the principle, first, that the committee shall have the power to call witnesses as it


may determine and, second, that the committee itself will decide what departments or what segments of a department it shall investigate.
The committee does that without any prior notice to the department concerned or indeed to the government itself. They break up into a number of sub-committees and a subcommittee will decide what branch of the government's operations it wishes to investigate. The sub-committee reports back to the main committee and the main committee then authorizes it to proceed in that way. I am making these remarks on the basis of a memorandum supplied to the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) by a member of the United Kingdom parliament.
The committee descends without warning on a government department and says, "We want you to tell us what you have in mind when you ask for this appropriation of X thousand pounds." The government department has no opportunity to prepare its case and it is not protected by the minister having the right to say what witnesses shall be heard by the committee or by the minister having the right to call upon only those departmental officials whom he is prepared to present.
That is a true outline of the conditions under which our committee was compelled to work last year and will be compelled to work this year under the terms of the reference we now have before us. We were confronted last year with the absurd situation that we did not have the power to call witnesses as a committee while the minister of the department under investigation had the power to say which of his officials would come and speak. The committee had no power to call witnesses while the minister was able to speak as a member of the committee and say, "I have decided that I shall get the deputy minister, or the director of this branch, or the director of that branch, but when he speaks he cannot speak as a witness, he speaks as the emanation of the minister." Those were the words used by the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration to describe the status of the officials of his department before the committee.
What more frustrating, what more absurd or ridiculous situation could a committee of this house be placed in? It simply could not come to grips with the department. It had to deal only with those who the minister said would be called before it. When they spoke, they spoke as emanations of the minister and, of course, they were bound to reflect and to defend the government's policy.
Whatever may be said as to the nature of this committee-and I am going to move

an amendment that the committee be empowered to send for persons, papers and records-I fancy it may be said by the Prime Minister, or by the Minister of Finance in his capacity as house leader, that this committee is still an experimental committee. I say to you, Mr. Speaker, that if this experiment does not succeed it will be a sorry day for parliament, and this committee will not succeed unless it is given a fair chance. The committee will not be given a fair chance unless it is allowed to do the job parliament and the country would like to see it do.
I wish to impress upon the government the fact that the United Kingdom parliament, the parliament of a country which is sometimes regarded as essentially, I was going to say "conservative" but if you do not like the word I will say "cautious", in its approach to such questions, when it set up a committee in 1912 with some misgivings from some members of that house, did not hesitate to give it all the powers it needed to do the job. The motion, as I have said, was introduced by the chancellor of the exchequer, Mr. Lloyd George. It was an experimental committee. It was a new departure, but they set it up with all the powers it needed. Here are the terms of reference of the United Kingdom committee, as found on page 360, volume 37, fifth series, of the United Kingdom Hansard. It was decided that a select committee be appointed to examine into and report on such of the estimates presented to the house as might seem fit to the committee. The committee had the power to decide which departments it would examine. After discussion, when the motion to set up the committee was carried, as a matter of course- as we find recorded in the United Kingdom Hansard-after the vote approving the committee had been carried, the question that the committee have power to send for persons, papers and records was put and agreed to.
So in that parliament, from which to a large extent we take the guiding principles of the procedures we follow here-and in this connection I suggest we could take a great deal of guidance for the work of this committee on estimates, because they do most important, far-reaching and beneficial work- they had no hesitation in giving this committee the power it needed to allow it to function in the interests of parliament as a whole, and not just in the interests of the government to be, what it can only otherwise be, a whitewash committee to defend the government's program as revealed through the estimates. They gave it the power to send for persons, papers and records, the first time they set it up. That was in 1912, 67509-104
Committee on Estimates and it is now 1956. Surely this government is not so reactionary that after 44 years of the example of what they do in the United Kingdom and all the benefits that will follow, they will refuse to give the committee of parliament the power to do what a committee of parliament should do.
I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Lanark (Mr. Blair):
That the motion be amended by adding thereto the following words:
"and that the said committee have power to send for persons, papers and records".

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we in this group are pleased that the government has submitted once again a proposal for a committee on estimates similar to the committee that was established last year. We shall be glad to support the motion.
We are also pleased that the hon. member for Kamloops has moved an amendment that would give the committee power to send for persons, papers and records. I shall say something on the amendment a little later in my remarks, but I should like first of all to say that we do not take the position that the committee on estimates takes the place of the committee of supply. No one tries to argue that, but at any rate we are glad to know it is recognized that in the last analysis it is the committee of supply, consisting of all the members in the house, that is responsible for every dollar that is to be voted by parliament. Nevertheless, despite the fact that the committee of supply is the most important cog in the machinery so far as the voting of money is concerned, we feel that it is a good idea that year by year a few departments should be referred to a committee on estimates.
One of the values to be gained from such a committee may not sound like a political value in the sense of the word which offended Your Honour a few moments ago. Nevertheless it is a real value. The study that takes place in a committee of this kind can be quite educational for the members of the committee and through them for members of the house as a whole. Indeed it can go even further than that. I am satisfied, indeed, that one of the real values of some of the important committees that have been held across the years has been in the education that has been afforded to members and through them to the country as a whole. I think of the excellent committee that we had a number of years ago on the question of old age security. I believe more came out of that committee than a mere recommendation; I think it was educational in its effect. Those who were on the external affairs committee last year, when General McNaughton and

Committee on Estimates other witnesses appeared before it to discuss matters in relation to our water supply and power resources, learned a great deal as a result of what went on in that committee. Similarly, it is an exceptionally good idea that a few departments each year can be scrutinized thoroughly and a few members become acquainted with the workings of those departments in the committee on estimates in a manner which is not possible in committee of supply.
However, it seems to me that the value of the estimates committee is greatly limited if it is not possible to call before the committee witnesses chosen by the committee itself. After all, if the only people who appear before that committee are those who are chosen by the minister, the value of that committee can be limited to such values as we get out of discussion here in the committee of supply. If members are going to learn what is going on, it seems to me they should have the right that is involved in the amendment that has been moved by the hon. member for Kamloops.
I think it is a fair question to ask, in this day and age, as to who is running the government in this country. Is it the cabinet or is it the civil service? I do not ask that question with malice aforethought, and I am fully conscious of our constitutional position, which specifies that the minister is completely responsible to parliament for all that goes on in his department, for the recommendations that he makes to parliament and for the positions that he may take on matters that are raised here on the floor of the house. Yet there are times when some of us wonder whether a particular minister exercises that responsibility merely by being the mouthpiece of civil servants who are behind him, civil servants whom we sometimes refer to, if we do not like their decisions, as bureaucrats. I know that the minister must protect civil servants and that it is the job of parliament to see that civil servants are protected, but I think the whole question of whether it is the cabinet or the civil service that is making the major policy decisions, that is really running the country, has become of such importance that it would be a good idea for the estimates committee to be able to call before it some of the senior civil servants and others in various departments so that they might be questioned along with the minister in order that we may, as I say, get this question sorted out as to who is really making some of the major decisions.
I do not think this is the time or the place to give examples and thereby to get into a discussion of one department or another. But all of us have various departments in mind where questions of the kind I have
[Mr. Knowles.}
alluded to might well be investigated. It seems to me that we would do well to have before the estimates committee some of the officials of the treasury board. It does seem to us that some of the most important decisions affecting government policy and national life are either made in treasury board or if there are policies or decisions that the government might like to consider they are vetoed or rejected by treasury board. I think it would be a good idea if we could have some of the senior officials of treasury board, and even intermediate officials, come before the estimates committee under the aegis of one department or another so that we could find out just how they work and who are making these major decisions.
I listened with interest to what the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) had to say regarding the practice of the estimates committee in the United Kingdom where it descends without warning on a particular department and inquires into its expenditures. I realize that that function is supposed to be performed by our treasury board, and I am satisfied that our treasury board does a good job in terms of checking the estimates of the various ministers to try to eliminate waste wherever possible and to try to cut down and avoid extravagance. But I confess that I am more concerned as to the part that treasury board plays in making major decisions of policy.
I find it very hard to discuss this matter in the abstract without at least mentioning some of the things in which some of us are interested. I could, for example, refer to questions such as increases in old age pensions or the question as to why it takes so long to get moving in the field of health insurance. I could raise the question of the pensions of superannuated civil servants or the question of the war veterans' allowance. I could raise any one of a dozen matters of this nature where what is involved is not waste or extravagance, in the terms in which my friends to the right so often use those words, but basic policy as to what the attitude of the country should be towards improvements in fields such as I have indicated.
I think it is a fair request that these people who are behind the ministers, and for whom the ministers, I admit, are responsible, should at least once in a while come before a committee of parliament so that we can find out whether the ministers are telling the civil service what they want or whether the civil service is telling the government what policies should be pursued. For these reasons, Mr. Speaker, I think, it

will be clear that we not only support the motion to establish a special committee on estimates but we would also like to see it given the wider scope that is involved in the amendment moved by the hon. member for Kamloops. Therefore we shall support the amendment and we shall support the establishing of the committee itself.

speakeroldname: Mr. W. Ross Thatcher (Moose Jaw-Lake Centre):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to speak very briefly on the motion now before us. I am one of those who support strongly the setting up of the estimates committee. I certainly feel that it did valuable work last year. It has always seemed to me that one of the chief duties of an elected representative is to thoroughly examine government expenditures to see that the taxpayers' dollar is being efficiently, properly and economically spent. Yet the experience I have had as a back-bencher is that there is no task in the house which is more frustrating, more disappointing, or more baffling, than the attempt to carry it out.
As hon. members know, under our British system of government, parliament is supposed to be supreme where finances are concerned. Yet in actual fact that theoretical supremacy is so ineffectively carried out, that I often wonder whether or not it actually exists. What are the reasons for this situation? I believe the main reason is due to the fact that our parliamentary machinery for examining the estimates is hopelessly outdated and outmoded. Our present method was formulated back in the days of confederation, and there have been very few improvements introduced into parliament since that time.
In the days of confederation, government had few financial complications. The government had little concern about national defence. It did not have to worry too much about social welfare. Things like the gold subsidy, the grain subsidy and so on did not enter into the picture. Back in 1868 the total budget of this parliament was $7-6 million. For the year 1874-75 the total of the estimates was still only $42 million. In 1910 the total of the estimates was $110 million. In 1913, the year before the war, the total budget was only $150 million.
I suggest that in those days it might have been possible for parliament to examine the estimates in the committee of supply, but times have changed. Canada has developed into a modern nation. Our population has increased many times, and government has become more complex. Today huge sums are spent for national defence, social welfare and the like. It is no exaggeration to say that 67509-104J
Committee on Estimates this year our budget will be almost $5 billion. On top of this sum, government crown corporations will be spending additional hundreds of millions of dollars. In other words, the government will be spending more than one-fifth of our whole gross national product. That means in effect, that today we are spending about 650 times what we spent in 1868. Yet the parliamentary machinery for examining these expenditures is relatively the same as it was back in the days of confederation.
When the estimates are tabled in the house, when this blue book is brought down and placed in front of hon. members, we are literally drowned in a morass of statistics and figures. I say that any hon. member in this house, no matter how diligent he may be, finds it physically impossible to do a thorough job of examining the estimates in addition to his other work.
I say further that our method in this parliament of examining estimates is so inefficient and so unbusinesslike as to be almost unbelievable. What is parliament's vehicle for examining the estimates? As you know, Mr. Speaker, the vehicle is the committee of the whole which in effect is the whole House of Commons with the Speaker out of the chair. The government introduces these estimates-perhaps 600 or 700 pages of them- to the committee of the whole. That committee is unwieldly, clumsy and hurried. It is hopelessly large. Usually questions are mixed up and bandied across the floor with regard to details, with regard to policy, with regard to amounts. Often there is little sequence to the questions. Some of them have little relation to each other. Often they do not even appear to be coherent. While it is true that members in the back benches can question cabinet members, nevertheless it is extremely difficult to secure the kind of information that a member should have.
Not only is this house poorly equipped to deal with estimates, Mr. Speaker, but more and more in recent years, it has been inclined to treat estimates as matters of secondary importance, that can be dealt with after all other business has been finished. I feel that the time allotted by the government for the debating of estimates is not satisfactory. We have now been sitting for about seven weeks and I think we have spent one day in discussing estimates. Far too often, it seems to me, the early weeks or months of a session of parliament are spent in debating relatively minor issues and later on the estimates are brought forward in a last-minute rush. In

Committee on Estimates the last session the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris), as reported at page 937 of Hansard of 1955, made this statement:
There has grown up In the country an impression that during the final week and especially on the final day, it has been our custom to pass large sums of money at a rate which is not in accordance with the seriousness of the subject. To my mind that opinion is false; . . .
In this connection I must say that I cannot agree with the Minister of Finance. Last year parliament had sat for five months. At the end of that five months' period it had passed only $189 million of estimates or 4-2 per cent of the total. The remainder was passed in the last few weeks. In the last week of the session of 1953-the last seven days-estimates totalling $866 million were put through. In the last week of the session of 1954, estimates totalling $2,715 million were put through. In the last week of the session of 1955 estimates totalling $563 million were put through. To anyone who studies the picture I think it is obvious that when estimates are passed with such speed they cannot possibly have been given by this parliament the kind of examination that they merit.
Who is to blame for the situation as it exists today? Since the government decides the order of business, I think it must accept a major share of the responsibility. In fairness I suppose I should say that the opposition is partly to blame because far too many of us are prone, early in the session, to make loquacious and sometimes repetitious speeches on matters which perhaps are not as important as are these estimates. Often the difficult but rather humdrum task of going over the accounts is neglected. I have a definite feeling that today, Mr. Speaker, it is not parliament which is the watchdog of the treasury, but rather it is a small group of civil servants. Even though those civil servants, mostly members of treasury board or the finance department do an effective job, I say that this is not a healthy situation. I think it exists only because private members of all parties, including the Liberal party, have permitted the control of the national purse to be gradually taken away from them.
The resolution before us tonight is going to improve the situation. I think it is a reform. It is at least going to mean that four departments will be thoroughly examined. But even if the resolution passes, as I know it will, I do not think parliament has gone far enough. I am still convinced that in this house too little use is made of standing committees. I think this fact is all the more regrettable because on the back benches, parliament has a great deal of effective

talent which is not being used. Many backbench members are able business and professional men. They come down here anxious to do a useful job. Yet usually they are not allotted specific work. I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that these back-bench members could be effectively used, if they were put on committees-particularly estimates committees-to go over and examine government spending. I believe that every single government expenditure should be referred to one standing committee or another. I believe that every department should be referred in a similar manner. For instance, agriculture estimates should go to the committee on agriculture. The estimates of the Department of Finance, the Department of National Revenue and the like should go to the banking and commerce committee. Perhaps there should be a special committee on defence to examine defence expenditures, veterans affairs expenditures and so on. Before any estimate is brought into this house I repeat, that I believe it should have been thoroughly checked and gone over by some standing committee. Certainly any private business, before spending money in the way in which we are spending it in this parliament, would make absolutely certain that the expenditures had been thoroughly justified.
Mr. Speaker, there is another field of government expenditure with respect to which I do not think parliament is doing its job. I refer to our crown corporations. I have been here since 1945. There are many crown corporations that I cannot remember ever having come before parliament, except in the committee of the whole for a five-minute or ten-minute examination, which was more or less routine. I am thinking at the moment of the Polymer Corporation, Canadian Arsenals Limited, Canadian Government Elevators, the printing bureau, the Canadian farm loan board and so on. Federal crown corporations today number 30, I believe. In those crown corporations the taxpayer has an investment of several billion dollars. Some of them from time to time go to the treasury for substantial subsidies. Yet today the average member of parliament has less knowledge of the operations of those corporations, than have many shareholders of ordinary companies. It is quite true that some of the crown corporations such as Trans-Canada Air Lines, the Canadian National Railways and, from time to time, the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation come before a parliamentary committee. But I say again to you tonight, Mr. Speaker, that that practice should be extended. Once a year every company owned by the government should be

obliged to come before one standing committee or another to be examined in detail.
I have one more suggestion to make tonight, Mr. Speaker, and I have made it in the past. It has always seemed to me that opposition members are handicapped in examining these estimates by a lack of research and technical assistance. Because of the time required by other parliamentary committees, without that assistance it is extremely difficult effectively to query experienced government officials. When a minister comes before the committee of supply or before a standing committee, invariably he is flanked by experts or by his officials, and their job is to justify the expenditures which the government is making. The opposition, on the other hand, has no such assistance. I think they could do their job a good deal better if they were given some kind of help in that regard. I believe that the importance of this committee which the minister is proposing to set up tonight cannot be exaggerated. It is a reform but it does not go far enough. It is a step in the right direction. It is going to mean that four departments will be examined, but in my opinion every department should be examined. Until we take such action parliament is not doing the job of examining estimates effectively.

The resolution which stands in the name of the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) reintroduces a practice which was begun last year and which was found useful. I should like to add what has been said already tonight in urging the Prime Minister and the members of the government, in fact all members of this house, to consider the amendment as a means of doing better what this resolution proposes to do.
Last year the estimates committee did perform a very useful function in more than one way; that has been pointed out already. Certainly it helped to educate the members of the house in the details of administration. It cleared a great many of the inquiries which otherwise would have been made on the floor in the committee of the whole. The proposal introduces a very minor extension of the powers of the committee, because basically the committee will be a committee of the house constituted in the same proportions as the house is constituted with the supporters of the government in the majority and therefore with the basic decisions of the committee under the control of the administration. As I say, the extension is relatively minor, but it seems to me that in last year's committee we had a useful instrument which could be substantially better if it had the power to inquire a little deeper, to go beneath the surface
Committee on Estimates and bring out the real facts on which the decisions of economical and effective administration must be based.
Now, I concede that there might be objections to giving the power to a committee to inquire into the affairs of the department about which some minister may be touchy. He may fear that opposition parties will seek partisan advantage by the exposure of maladministration. I think if any member of this house, in fact if any member of this government will look at the matter fairly and [DOT]clearly, it redounds to the advantage of the government basically to improve the administration because the government takes the final responsibility for the quality and character of the administration which goes on in the various departments of government. If that administration can be improved through the medium of a committee of this house or by giving a committee more power to make such improvements, then in the long run the advantage will accrue to the government of the day as well as to parliament as a whole in the discharge of its traditional function of voting the funds the administration requires to carry on its duties.
In supporting this I do suggest that the members of the government regard this as one means of doing more effectively what has been done fairly well in some instances in the past, not only to the credit of this house and the committee but to the credit of the government itself whose administration can thereby be improved.

I wish to associate myself, Mr. Speaker, with those who have spoken earlier in asking that the powers of this committee be extended. I remember the committee last year, in its initial year, and I have a very clear recollection of the manner in which the committee found its work hampered by the lack of the power which is requested in the amendment submitted by the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton). I think perhaps that some of us who sit in this house have become, shall I say, rather insulated from public opinion and fail to realize that this institution of parliament is now on trial in the public mind. I think it is not too much to say that there is a most deplorable and dangerous attitude of cynicism towards parliament as a vehicle of democracy today.
I wonder sometimes if the reason for that is not to be found in the state of affairs that was described to me by a very eminent Canadian citizen who at one time sat in this house. He remarked to me that there is a popular illusion we have a government, whereas the real fact of the matter is that

Committee on Estimates we have an administration with a political front. I submit, sir, that is a very dangerous situation. One of the ways in which this cynical attitude towards parliament can perhaps he dissipated is by parliament to display the intention of really examining the work that is done in its name, and revealing to the general public the results of that examination.
Sometimes it has been changes of procedure of an apparently minor character that have very drastically altered the whole structure of parliament. One could recall, for instance, that it was purely the accident of a monarch being unable to speak the English language that set up the beginnings of our cabinet system as we know it today. We should be very careful, sir, not to imagine that our very new institution of parliament, and it is a very new institution in the shape it has taken today, is one which could not very well be deprived of real effective power, not through any deliberate action on the part of its members but by the failure to realize the danger points in our procedure. I suggest to you, sir, that one of the most grave danger points is when the government of the day, the executive of this parliament, is afraid to entrust to a committee of this house the power to examine ruthlessly, without let or hindrance, into all the actions that are taken in the name of this parliament.

I should like to add a word to what has been said in favour of the amendment. I think if any intelligent stranger were in the gallery, and I am sure there are plenty here tonight, and had listened to this amendment he would have said "Well, that is the most reasonable thing I ever heard; why would they not do it?" As I listened to the hon. member for St. Paul's (Mr. Michener) and the hon. member from farther west, I felt that way. I have got to my feet merely to say this. If the amendment is turned down, and we have some reason to think it will be by what I believe the great Disraeli once referred to as brute votes, I hope it will not be turned down without reason given. I hope it will not be turned down in the ordinary, rather mechanical way that we are so often denied what we ask. I do hope that reasons, or what hon. gentlemen opposite regard as reasons, will be given as to why this suggestion, so eminently reasonable on the face of it and in the light of the experience we have had in this house, is to be turned down. I hope every effort will be made to state a case against these reasonable arguments.

Mr. Speaker,
I do not wish to take up the time of the house in making remarks in this regard that have 

already been made. I agree with the hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre (Mr. Thatcher) who said that the increased complexity of government since 1867 has made the proper examination of estimates in the committee of supply a virtual impossibility. Since 1867 government has become increasingly complex. Government departments have grown to such an extent that in effect most government departments are, through the very necessity of our modern way of life, run by civil servants. As a result it is almost impossible for any cabinet minister, no matter how brilliant and capable he might be, to fully understand and have complete knowledge of all the work of other government departments if for no other reason than the fact that cabinet ministers frequently change from one portfolio to another.
The present system we have in committee of supply is, of course, as every hon. member knows, that the minister is there usually with one or two assistants to advise him and to answer questions from hon. members of either the opposition or the government. Very often, in fact very often indeed, the questions which are asked are extremely detailed and the minister is unable to answer them and the assistants are unable to supply him with the information immediately. Consequently, the minister will acknowledge the question and say, "We can answer it tomorrow or the next day", and will undertake to furnish the information at a later date. I am sure many hon. members have had the experience of having this information supplied as the minister promised but often several months after the question was asked and frequently after the house has closed. I am not criticizing the ministers for this for I realize the complexity of their job and its great scope. Frequently, it is impossible to get the answers right away but it certainly is not very helpful for the proper examination of the estimates in the house.
The present committee the government is setting up is certainly a step in the right direction. Having been a member of the estimates committee for some of the time during the last session, I think it certainly is a help and a step in the right direction, but the suggestion of the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton), which has been supported by other hon. members on this side of the house, is indeed an even farther step in the right direction.
Last year when the estimates of certain branches of the government were referred to the special committee on estimates the result was very much the same as what happens in the committee of supply. The government called or made available as witnesses various senior civil servants who had a considerable

knowledge of the departments from which they came. Some of them, however, are undoubtedly in the same position as cabinet ministers in that their departments are now so large it is almost impossible, even for senior civil servants who have been in the department for many years, to know all the facts about their own departments. As a result, last year in the committee on estimates questions which were asked frequently had to be put over until the next day in order that the answers could be looked up or some other official consulted. To a lesser degree, but sufficiently seriously so that it is almost in the same position, the same problem exists in the estimates committee which exists in the committee of supply.
If the committee on estimates were em-powdered to call witnesses before the committee and any particular witnesses that the members of the committee desired to have called, I am sure we would get a much more capable and complete examination of the estimates of this house.

Mr. Speaker, I too will take only a few minutes of the house's time tonight in connection with this matter. Had I not heard the remarks of the hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre I perhaps would not have said anything at this time. However, the hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre (Mr. Thatcher) referred at some length to the fact that many people here did not take a very active part in connection with the estimates which came before the committee of the whole, and perhaps that was because there was not ample opportunity to do so. I think that was perhaps an unwarranted criticism. When I think back to the many hours that I have stood on my feet in this house in connection with continual examination in relation to transport and national defence last year I feel there was plenty of opportunity and if people wanted to inquire into those estimates they had the chance to get to their feet.
That, of course, does not mean that we are going to obtain the answers which we should get. It seems to me that the hon. member for Oxford put his finger on one of the major problems, that is, in the examination we are constantly faced with a frustrating situation where we have two or three people standing between us and the person we are examining and it is most difficult to get a straight answer under circumstances of that kind. I do not think anyone who has not been accustomed to conducting examinations wherein one questions a witness directly can appreciate the frustration that arises in the house as one watches these conversations which take place between the minister and the experts
Committee on Estimates who sit before him. As long as that condition exists we are not going to be able to carry out a proper examination in this house and therefore any move which will give us an opportunity to examine the parties directly is going to be a step in the right direction.
A second point I would make is that we have reached a stage where nearly half of the total estimates refer to the Department of National Defence. If we are going to have a continuation of the policy as I have seen it here of getting down finally to the place where we get no answer whatsoever on the basis of security, and this has happened time after time, then the work of the opposition is going to become almost unbearable.
I think we all feel that conditions of security are most important. I would be the last one to suggest that we should cut away any cloak of secrecy that is required, but when you talk about frustration I must point out it is really frustrating to find that an answer is refused you in the house and when you pick up the newspaper next day, or Time magazine the next month, you find the answer that you could not get right in this very chamber. It seems to me that if there were an opportunity of examining the large masses of defence expenditures on the basis of direct question of the people involved there would be ample opportunity to discern very easily those matters on which we might be entitled to information and those matters on which, for obvious reasons of security, we should not be allowed to ask for the production of papers or witnesses.
As long as this portion of the estimates continues to climb and to amount to almost 50 per cent of the total budget, then I say a step must be taken along that line as well.
In connection with the suggestion of the hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre, that we perhaps need some assistance, I would say this. Give us the vehicle here to enable us to get close to the problem and I am satisfied that there are people quite capable of conducting a thorough examination. I am quite satisfied also that there are those qualified in accounting and the other professions who will enable us to do a good job. All we have to have is an indication from the government that they are prepared to really face close scrutiny in connection with these expenditures.

In the United Kingdom the practice is for certain departments or even certain sections of departments to be selected for this purpose.
The rotation of departments is a good thing if we are not going to have the estimates of all departments reviewed in select committees. There is a great benefit to be achieved in the control of government expenditures by preserving so far as possible the element of surprise in the selection of the particular departments, sections or crown corporations whose estimates are to be reviewed in detail. There is such a thing as a department being so well prepared defensively on their estimates that they sometimes defeat the general purpose that a committee on estimates can help to serve in relation to all departments.

I know, and I am referring to that as a useful guide. I will come in my remarks to the estimates committee at Westminster. I am pointing out here that the practice at Westminster in relation to the public accounts committee is a useful practice. In these committees, in the case of the public accounts committee, in the case of the estimates committee, indeed in the case of a good many other committees, it is the opposition members on those committees who do the work. Government members as a rule are

not interested in probing into expenditures or estimates. It is left to the members of the opposition to do that investigatory work. We have not reached the point here, of course, where the opposition is permitted to make the selection, even in the interests of a strict review of proposed departmental expenditures. The opposition did propose to the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) at this session that four departments should be selected for review in the committee on estimates, namely the Departments of National Defence, Trade and Commerce, Justice and Fisheries. The Department of National Defence is one that naturally suggests itself because of the extent of the expenditure in that department. The others are important departments, and at this particular time there is much to be said for taking the estimates of these departments before the committee on estimates.
But the government would not accede to that proposal, so we come to the second alternative, the one that is in effect here. It is that the government selects the particular departments whose estimates are to be referred to the committee. It is a strange thing, it is an anomalous situation indeed and one that could be found I am sure only in a House of Commons completely dominated by the government as the majority in this house has been dominated by the government, that a committee set up for the purpose of investigating and inquiring into proposed government expenditures is to have its work controlled for it by the government'. Think of it, sir, it is the government's administration; it is the government's estimates that are to be reviewed by this committee. Nevertheless, if the majority in this house remains submissive to the will of the government, the government will decide what amongst its estimates this committee will be permitted to review. I say you could not have a more effective hamstringing of the work of a committee on estimates than that. I urge upon the house that this committee is not going to be given an opportunity to do the effective work that needs to be done by a committee on estimates if the government is simply to dictate to the committee in the manner now proposed the work that is to come before it.
I come to the third alternative, sir. It is the alternative that the committee itself, instead of the government, should make the selection. We have been told by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris), as leader of the house, in his very brief remarks on February 9 at pages 1041 and 1042 of Hansard when introducing this resolution, that the estimates of the Departments of Labour, National Health and Welfare, National Revenue and Post Office are to be referred to this committee. This is the government's decision, the
Committee on Estimates government's selection. The committee itself is to have no opportunity to make a selection. I point out to this house that the committee on estimates at Westminster, a committee which we are told has functioned very satisfactorily in the opinion of all political parties since 1912, has the power to select the work it will do. It is not a case of dictation from the government and reference to that committee. The committee, being a standing committee, makes its own selections of the departments whose estimates it chooses to review. This preserves the freedom of the committee. It preserves the valuable element of surprise in reference to all government departments.
I imagine the Minister of Finance will be prepared to recognize the benefit of surprise in an undertaking of this kind because a great deal of his work is concerned with a similar responsibility of reviewing the estimates of other departments. We know from last year's experience in the committee that the minister whose estimates are under review has a great deal to say about the procedure to be followed in the committee. Here, we have a situation where the government is making the selections of the departments. I say that at the very least the committee should have the right to make its own decisions. I am not overlooking the fact the government is going to have a majority on this committee, but in relation to the exercise by that majority of its function in the committee I say that due regard should be had to the proposals put forward by opposition members in that committee.
Now, we are told that this committee is still in the experimental stages. It has been quite evident, sir, that there has been a division of feeling in the cabinet on this matter. There are some ministers who are prepared to be modern and bring their estimates before a proper committee on estimates. On the other hand, there are ministers here who have become so accustomed to the privileges and powers they enjoy that they look with the utmost disfavour on any proposal that their estimates should be brought under detailed review in any manner by a select committee of the house such as the committee on estimates.
The committee to which I am referring at Westminster is a committee of 36 members which divides itself into five subcommittees. Those committees carry on their detailed examination and sit extensively during the session. Indeed, sometimes they have sat while the house was not in session-even after the conclusion of the session. They make their own selection of the particular department, crown corporation, section or agency

Committee on Estimates they are going to investigate and that has been a most useful procedure.
In the interests of good government, in the interests of the control of expenditure, I say that the committee would do well to ponder these following words. I shall give the reference after I have read the words, Mr. Speaker.
If the order of reference is not wide enough and does not go far enough I suggest to the minister that it should be widened. This is something new; it is an experiment. If in the government's mind it is a reform let us treat it as a reform and see that it is properly framed so that it operates. If it is only a concession to my hon. friends of the opposition then let us make our concession freely and willingly, not grudgingly.
And further:
Nevertheless the control, criticism, and scrutiny of the estimates is one of the bulwarks of the opposition. The opposition should, if it is doing its duty, take every possible step to see to it that these expenditures are appropriate and in the interests of the country. May I say as one who enjoyed being in the opposition for two parliaments that I have great sympathy for the opposition, and believe it is the duty of the government and the house to give the opposition every opportunity to scrutinize these estimates.
Those references may be found on pages 953 and 854 of Hansard, February 8, 1955.
Those words are not the words of a member of Her Majesty's loyal opposition. Those were words uttered in the debate on the corresponding government motion a year ago by the then hon. member for Quebec South, Mr. Power. I commend his words, not only to his successor but also to the Prime Minister, and I repeat the concluding remarks of Mr. Power when he said that he believed it is the duty of the government and the house to give the opposition every opportunity to scrutinize these estimates.
Mr. Speaker, does any member of the government seriously pretend that the opposition is given every opportunity to scrutinize the estimates when the government will not give the committee power to send for persons, papers and records-I say no more on that- or to give it power to select the business that it is to do? Is it giving the opposition the opportunity that Mr. Power recognized that it ought to have in the interests of good government when the government says, "We will decide what business shall be permitted to come before that committee on estimates and by the same token we will decide what estimates shall not come before that committee on estimates"? That is the position of the government to date in this debate. It is going to select the business to come before that committee.
I made mention of the way the committee on estimates functions at Westminster. The committee there decides what estimates-
May I ask the hon. member a question, Mr. Speaker? I should like to ask him if when the Conservatives were in power there was a committee on estimates?

In Britain? I am sorry the hon. member has not been following the debate. It has been said by other hon. members and I said it not more than five minutes ago, that the committee on estimates has been a standing committee of the House of Commons at Westminster since 1912, and its function-
I meant when the Conservatives were in power in this house; was there a committee on estimates?
Perhaps he cannot remember that far back.

No, there was not, but I will tell the hon. member that the expenditure in those days was just 10 per cent of what it is today. In other words, that is a 900 per cent reason why there ought now to be an effective committee on estimates.
Is it a matter of figures or is it a matter of principle?

I think the hon. member, if he is concerned about the matter of principle, is apparently going to have to ask himself whether he even condescends to approve of the introduction of the motion to set up even this truncated and deformed committee on estimates. These members are so brave, Mr. Speaker, until they are called upon to make a speech and I suggest-

Office of The Prime Minister and President of the Council
Toronto, Ontario, February 22, 1956.
Dear Mr. Prime Minister:
This will acknowledge receipt of your letter of February 20, 1956 on the proposed fiscal arrangements and the attached memorandum of answers of the Minister of Finance for Canada to the questions raised by the provinces.
Certain features of the proposal referred to in your letter and in the memorandum of the Minister of Finance are improvements over the present fiscal arrangements, but it appears to us that the basic formula which uses the weighted average of the per capita tax yields of only Ontario and British Columbia-to all intents and purposes this means Ontario-does not recognize the heavy financial burdens that are imposed on this province and its municipalities in servicing a rapidly growing population and industry which produce such a large proportion of the federal government's revenue. In view of the enormous obligations and commitments that we face, we feel strongly that a formula that provides a special payment to all the provinces except Ontario fails to meet the special needs of this province. As a first step in this approach, we believe that the equalization payments should be calculated on the basis of the four provinces having the highest per capita tax yields.
We shall be glad to meet with you, your colleagues and representatives of the other provinces in a resumption of the conference preferably on March 9.
Yours very sincerely, LESLIE M. FROST

My dear Prime Minister:
Your letter of February 2, 1956 and the memorandum from your Minister of Finance giving answers to a number of questions raised by treasury officials are acknowledged.
If a further meeting in committee is found generally desirable, I shall be glad to attend it. If, however, no general meeting is to take place, then I must press for a conference between our respective governments, further to discuss the terms of the proposed agreement, insofar as they apply to a province like British Columbia which is not dependent upon fiscal subsidies; is experiencing an unprecedented economic growth; and requires a greater allocation from the cultivation of income tax fields to keep pace with a development which, apart from its provincial worth, will yield vast returns to the nation.
Your letter indicates that discussions with the individual provinces will be conducted by yourself and Mr. Harris on behalf of the federal government. Mr. Bonner, our attorney general and I will represent British Columbia, and on the assumption that technical staff will be present, I propose taking with me Messrs. Fisher and Gunderson, and possibly Mr. Veitch.
Our current session of the legislature will not terminate its labours until the second week in March. I would, therefore, urge that our meeting do not take place before March 9, 1956.
The memorandum from Mr. Harris is being studied and comments thereon will be made either before or at the meeting suggested.
Yours faithfully,
